t: Why You Shouldn't Pep-Talk Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/09/21/why-you-shouldnt-pep-talk-difficult-students/
q: The student stands wordlessly, eyes averted, still smarting from yet another backslide as the earnest teacher softens the blows of the student’s many transgressions.
But pulling difficult students aside for pep-talks, particularly in response to recent misbehavior, will not only delay real and lasting improvement, but it can cause behavior to worsen.

Most difficult students have a history of misbehavior reaching as far back as preschool. Add the near-constant flow of pep-talks over the years, and you have a group of students who have heard it all.
When difficult students see how desperate you are for them to improve, you hand over much of the leverage you need to help them change their ways.

Eye contact and a nod from across the room, a knowing smile and a fist bump, a note folded over and waiting on their desk . . . these authentic moments between you mean the world to students labeled as “difficult.

t: Why You Should Never, Ever Confuse Accountability And Motivation ntability-and-motivation/
q: One reason many teachers struggle with classroom management is because they confuse motivation and accountability.
There are only two effective ways to hold students accountable. The first, which is a response to individual misbehavior, is to dispassionately follow your classroom management plan.
Both ways are action-oriented. In other words, you do something in response to misbehavior, which is a key characteristic of effective accountability.
Sometimes this tact is used in place of accountability and sometimes it’s used in addition to accountability—as in escorting a student to time-out while giving a lecture.
True accountability, on the other hand, as defined above, protects the student-teacher relationship. It’s never personal or hurtful.
Motivation, in an effective classroom management sense, is never negative and comes more from the classroom environment you keep than the words you use.
And it never, ever replaces, hinders, or weakens true accountability.
x: There are only two legitimate forms of accountability: enforcing a consequence per your classroom management plan, or stopping and restarting a class-wide routine that wasn't performed correctly.

He defines true accountability as strictly action-oriented—following a classroom management plan to enforce a consequence, or stopping and restarting a botched class-wide routine—with talk held to a minimum.
Effective accountability is action-oriented with minimal talk; substituting lectures, threats, or arguments for action undermines the process.
Mixing accountability and motivation (e.g., lecturing while walking a student to time-out) damages trust and increases misbehavior.

q: Small, seemingly insignificant behaviors in September will in almost every circumstance multiply into major disruptions down the road.

The second common approach that leads to growing and pervading misbehavior is when teachers are unclear about what they expect from students. This is the “I’ll know it when I see it” approach.
The lesson here is that you can’t effectively hold students accountable for that which hasn’t been clearly and thoroughly defined for them.

The solution to both faulty approaches is to take the time to thoroughly teach what you expect from your students, from A to Z and back again, based on the clarity of what you want each day to look like.
